title: How to document ‘process of experimentation’ for tax purposes
description: Document the process of experimentation with contemporaneous, business-component-level records showing at least 80% of activities evaluated alternatives.
summary: Documenting the process of experimentation for the federal R&D tax credit requires U.S. taxpayers to keep contemporaneous, business-component-level records showing at least 80% of research activities formed a systematic evaluation of alternatives under IRC Section 41(d). Recent IRS refund-claim rules, revised Form 6765 Section G, and Phoenix Design Group make hypothesis logs, failed-trial records, and task-level time tracking essential.

body.text: Documenting the process of experimentation for the federal R&D tax credit requires U.S. taxpayers to keep contemporaneous, business-component-level records showing at least 80% of research activities formed a systematic evaluation of alternatives under IRC Section 41(d). Recent IRS refund-claim rules, revised Form 6765 Section G, and Phoenix Design Group make hypothesis logs, failed-trial records, and task-level time tracking essential.

Documenting the "process of experimentation" (PoE) is the central evidentiary requirement for substantiating the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities (commonly known as the research and development, or R&D, tax credit) under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(5). Under United States federal income tax law, achieving a novel commercial product, completing a complex capital project, or solving a difficult engineering problem is insufficient on its own to qualify for the credit. Instead, a taxpayer must demonstrate through contemporaneous, project-level and activity-level records that at least 80% ("substantially all") of the research activities undertaken for each distinct business component constituted elements of a structured, evaluative process—anchored in the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science—designed to evaluate one or more alternatives and eliminate specific technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design.

Recent judicial decisions and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) administrative reforms have fundamentally transformed PoE documentation from a retrospective audit-defense exercise into a front-end filing prerequisite. In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (decided December 23, 2024), the United States Tax Court disallowed claimed R&D credits across all sampled engineering projects and sustained 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC Section 6662 because the taxpayer relied on linear design stages, standard engineering calculations, and generalized timesheets rather than contemporaneous records demonstrating an iterative evaluation of technical alternatives. Concurrently, following procedural litigation over refund-claim specificity in Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-CV-890-TS-CMR (D. Utah July 15, 2021), the IRS instituted mandatory upfront refund-claim disclosures via Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F and News Release IR-2021-203 (subsequently refined effective June 18, 2024, to require business component identification, research activity descriptions, and qualified expense totals at the time of filing) and overhauled Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) to mandate component-level reporting in Section G for tax years beginning after 2025.
I. Statutory and Regulatory Foundation of the Process of Experimentation
A. The Statutory Mandate and the Resolution of Technical Uncertainty

Under IRC Section 41(d)(1) (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(2) (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)), research activities constitute qualified research only if substantially all of the activities are elements of a process of experimentation relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a business component. The statute mandates that the research be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, the application of which is intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(A) and (B), these qualification rules must be applied separately to each "business component," which the statute defines as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer.

At the center of this statutory architecture is the requirement to identify and resolve objective technical uncertainty. Pursuant to Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) and Section 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) (promulgated in Treasury Decision 9104, effective January 2, 2004, applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information only if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. The Treasury Regulations establish a three-prong legal standard for technical uncertainty: uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer at the outset of the research activities does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of that business component. Consequently, even where a taxpayer knows at the outset of a project that a technical objective is achievable in terms of basic capability and general method, a valid process of experimentation may still occur if the appropriate design required to achieve that technical result remains uncertain when research activities begin.

Two points of regulatory precision govern how existing public knowledge and reliance on hard sciences interact with the uncertainty standard. First, under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), proving that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering technological information does not require the taxpayer to seek information that "exceeds, expands or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering". However, as recent U.S. Tax Court jurisprudence demonstrates, if the information already available to the taxpayer—whether through existing public literature, vendor specifications, historical project archives, or standard engineering equations—readily establishes the appropriate design at the outset, then objective technical uncertainty does not exist, and routine design iteration or general project complexity will be disallowed. Second, under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(4), the process of experimentation used to discover information must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. While technical compliance discussions frequently reference chemistry alongside these disciplines, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(4) formally enumerates those four statutory categories—with chemistry encompassed within the physical sciences—and explicitly states that a taxpayer "may employ existing technologies and may rely on existing principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science to satisfy this requirement".
B. The Systematic Hypothesis-Trial-Evaluation Cycle and the Dual 80% Thresholds

To satisfy Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a taxpayer cannot merely demonstrate that technical uncertainty existed at the inception of a project and was eventually resolved. The regulation explicitly provides that uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component "does not establish that all activities undertaken to achieve that new or improved business component constitute a process of experimentation". Instead, the taxpayer must execute and contemporaneously document a structured, evaluative process encompassing three mandatory regulatory elements. First, the taxpayer must isolate the specific technical unknowns regarding capability, method, or appropriate design concerning the development or improvement of the business component. Second, the taxpayer must formulate one or more technical alternatives—structured as testable hypotheses or candidate designs—intended to eliminate that specific uncertainty. Third, the taxpayer must design and conduct a systematic process of evaluating those alternatives, such as through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error procedure, that is generally capable of evaluating more than one alternative.

As reinforced by the legislative history to the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 99-841, at II-72), the IRS Software Process of Experimentation Audit Guidelines (May 2005), and federal appellate precedent in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), this evaluative sequence operationalizes the scientific method in an industrial or commercial setting: formulating a hypothesis that links a manipulated technical variable to an expected performance outcome, conducting structured trials to test the hypothesis, analyzing the resulting empirical data, and refining or discarding the hypothesis based on those results.

Crucially, under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-1(a) and Section 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), eligibility for the R&D tax credit does not require the taxpayer to succeed in developing the new or improved business component. Broad retrospective summaries stating that an engineering group built a new system or improved an existing product line fail under IRS examination because they describe only the commercial endpoint while omitting the intermediate experimental steps. Conversely, recording rejected design alternatives, failed prototypes, and negative test results provides direct, objective evidence that the appropriate design was uncertain at the outset and that a systematic trial-and-error evaluation actually occurred.

Furthermore, taxpayers must quantitatively substantiate two distinct 80% ("substantially all") thresholds established by the Internal Revenue Code and Treasury Regulations. First, under the activity-level "substantially all" test for the Process of Experimentation (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)), for a business component's research activities to constitute qualified research under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C), 80% or more of the taxpayer's research activities with respect to that business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, and determined without regard to the employee wage rule of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(2)—must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose under IRC Section 41(d)(3). As confirmed by the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal, the denominator of this 80% fraction consists of all research activities for the business component whose expenses are deductible under Section 174 (or domestic research expenditures under Section 174A, satisfying IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A)) and that are not excluded under IRC Section 41(d)(4), while the numerator consists of those research activities that constitute elements of a process of experimentation:
Component PoE Ratio = (Research Activities Constituting Elements of a Process of Experimentation) ÷ (Total Section 174 / 174A Research Activities Not Excluded Under IRC § 41(d)(4)) ≥ 80%

If the ≥ 80% threshold is satisfied for a business component, the remaining 20% or less of research activities for that component also qualify as part of the credit calculation, provided they satisfy IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) and are not excluded under IRC Section 41(d)(4). Conversely, if the component's experimental activities fall below 80% (for example, 75%), the entire business component fails to qualify unless the taxpayer can isolate a qualifying subcomponent under the shrinking-back rule of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2).

Second, under the employee-level "substantially all" test for wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)), which operates independently of the component-level PoE test, if at least 80% of an individual employee's total services performed for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of "qualified services" (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research), then 100% of that employee's taxable wages for the year qualify as in-house research expenses. If an employee's qualified services fall below 80% (for example, 79%), only the exact pro-rata ratio of time actually spent performing qualified services to total time worked may be included in qualified wages under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(1).
C. The Contemporaneous Recordkeeping Mandate and Cost Nexus

Substantiating the Process of Experimentation requires contemporaneous documentation—records generated and maintained concurrently with the performance of the research activities rather than reconstructed retrospectively during tax return preparation or audit defense. The statutory and regulatory authority for this requirement rests on IRC Section 6001, Treasury Regulation Section 1.6001-1(a) and (e), and the R&D credit-specific recordkeeping mandate in Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(d). Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.6001-1(a), every person subject to income tax must keep permanent books of account or records sufficient to establish the amount of gross income, deductions, credits, or other matters required to be shown on any return, and under Section 1.41-4(d), a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC Section 41 "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit".

As detailed in the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG) (LMSB-04-0508-030, May 2008) and Chapter 7 of the Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities IRC § 41 (June 2005), failure to maintain adequate records linking Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) to Qualified Research Activities (QRAs) at the business-component level creates a fatal "nexus problem". When taxpayers accumulate costs solely by department or cost center and apply retrospective percentage estimates to employee wages without contemporaneous records tying specific employee hours to specific experimental steps, IRS examiners are instructed to disallow the claim as un-auditable. Under federal judicial precedent—including Shami v. Commissioner, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014), and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113—courts will not apply the Cohan estimation rule unless the taxpayer first establishes through credible, objective evidence that qualified research activities satisfying IRC Section 41(d) actually occurred, and subjectively reconstructed post-hoc testimony is rejected when unsupported by contemporaneous project artifacts.
II. The Regulatory, Procedural, and Litigation Landscape
A. The Cumulative Four-Part Test Under IRC Section 41(d)

The Process of Experimentation does not operate in isolation; it is one of four cumulative statutory tests under IRC Section 41(d)(1) that must be satisfied separately for each business component. If a taxpayer fails to substantiate any single criterion for a claimed business component, the entire component fails to qualify at that level, forcing the taxpayer to rely on the "shrinking-back rule" of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2). Under the shrinking-back rule, the four-part test is applied iteratively to the "most significant subset" of elements (subcomponents) of the larger component, which can salvage partial eligibility only if the taxpayer has maintained granular technical and time-tracking documentation at the subcomponent level. The table below aligns the four cumulative statutory tests with their exact legal citations, substantive standards, and primary contemporaneous audit substantiation artifacts.

cells: 1. Permitted Purpose (Business Component Test)
IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii); IRC § 41(d)(2)(B); IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)–(B); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii) & (a)(5)(ii)

Research application must be intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component (product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention) relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (excluding style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors).

Project authorizations, functional specifications, design requirements, and work orders identifying the discrete business component (or subcomponent under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) and the specific functional or performance metric targeted for improvement.
2. Elimination of Uncertainty (Section 174 / 174A Test)

Expenditures must qualify as domestic research or experimental costs incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business to discover information that eliminates technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design as of the beginning of research activities.

Pre-project technical scoping memos, literature/patent reviews, and design review minutes establishing that information available to the taxpayer at project inception could not establish capability, method, or appropriate design.
3. Technological in Nature (Discovering Technological Information Test)

Research must be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature, meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Engineering calculations, chemical/physical formulas, computer science architecture specs, and researcher qualifications demonstrating reliance on hard sciences rather than social sciences, management studies, or aesthetic design.
4. Process of Experimentation (Substantially All Test)

Substantially all (≥ 80%) of the research activities for each business component must constitute elements of a systematic, evaluative process (e.g., modeling, simulation, or systematic trial-and-error) capable of evaluating one or more alternatives to resolve the uncertainty.

Time-stamped records of the hypothesis-trial-analysis cycle, simulation logs, prototype test data, records of failed iterations/rejected alternatives, and granular time logs demonstrating that ≥ 80% of component research activity was experimental.

For tax years beginning before January 1, 2022, IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) cross-referenced current deductions under former IRC Section 174; for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Pub. L. 115-97) mandated 5-year domestic (and 15-year foreign) amortization of Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures under IRC Section 174. Following subsequent legislative updates reflected in current 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) and the December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765, domestic research or experimental expenditures are referenced under IRC Section 174A, while preserving the underlying substantive requirement under Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(1) and Section 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) that activities seek to eliminate technical uncertainty in the experimental or laboratory sense.
B. Heightened IRS Procedural Scrutiny: IR-2021-203, the June 2024 Waiver, Form 6765 Section G, and Premier Tech

Over the past five years, the IRS has systematically shifted the compliance burden from post-filing audit examination to upfront procedural validation at the moment an original return or amended refund claim is filed. Evaluating this administrative regime requires distinguishing between the judicial holding in Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States and the IRS's subsequent administrative and regulatory countermeasures.
1. Judicial Holding vs. Administrative Countermeasures Following Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States

While practitioner discussions occasionally characterize Premier Tech as a case where a claim suffered judicial dismissal for lacking project-level specificity, the federal district court actually ruled against the IRS and in favor of the taxpayer—a judicial defeat that directly catalyzed the IRS's current upfront disclosure regime. In Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-CV-890-TS-CMR, 2021 WL 2982064 (D. Utah July 15, 2021), a Utah-based corporation filed an amended corporate income tax return (Form 1120X) attaching a completed Form 6765 claiming a $190,263 federal R&D tax credit refund. The IRS administratively denied the refund and moved to dismiss the taxpayer's subsequent federal lawsuit for lack of jurisdiction, arguing that under the specificity requirement of Treasury Regulation Section 301.6402-2(b)(1), the claim was procedurally invalid because the taxpayer had not attached project-level descriptions of the research conducted, the business components developed, and the employee wages and supplies tied to specific projects.

United States District Judge Ted Stewart denied the government's motion to dismiss, holding that Premier Tech's completed Form 6765 and Form 1120X satisfied Treasury Regulation Section 301.6402-2(b)(1). The district court observed that Form 6765 (as structured at that time) asked only for quantitative totals and did not request project-level narratives, reasoning that "if the IRS wants more information about the research tax credits, the IRS could require that information on Form 6765," and warning that demanding extra documentation beyond official form instructions could "lead to absurd and patently unfair results for taxpayers". Rather than accepting that a bare numeric Form 6765 suffices, the IRS responded to the July 15, 2021 Premier Tech opinion exactly three months later—on October 15, 2021—by issuing Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F and News Release IR-2021-203, and subsequently redesigning Form 6765 to add Section G. Specifically, Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F instructed IRS classifiers to screen refund claims at the processing campus level and reject deficient claims upfront before initiating an examination, thereby preventing taxpayers from invoking the judicial "waiver doctrine" (which had defeated the government the day after Premier Tech in Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-cv-00501 (D. Utah July 16, 2021)).
2. IR-2021-203 and the June 18, 2024 Refund Claim Modifications

Under News Release IR-2021-203 (October 15, 2021) and Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F, for any amended return or claim for refund involving an IRC Section 41 research credit filed after January 10, 2022, the IRS initially mandated five items of factual information at filing to satisfy Treasury Regulation Section 301.6402-2(b)(1). However, effective for claims postmarked or dated June 18, 2024 and subsequent (codified in the IRS Frequently Asked Questions on Section 41 Amended Returns and Internal Revenue Manual IRM 4.46.3.7.6 and IRM 21.7.4), the IRS waived the requirement to provide two employee-specific items at the time of filing: (a) the names of the individuals who performed each research activity, and (b) the information each individual sought to discover. The IRS explicitly cautions that both waived items must still be maintained in the taxpayer's records and may be requested if a refund claim is selected for examination.

Following the June 18, 2024 modification, every research credit claim for refund must provide three mandatory categories of factual information at the time of filing, verified by a written declaration signed under penalties of perjury and submitted on paper or via facsimile, as the IRS does not accept portable electronic storage devices such as USB drives. First, the taxpayer must identify all business components (as defined in IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B)) that form the factual basis of the research credit claim for the claim year. Second, for each business component, the taxpayer must describe all research activities performed, specifically detailing what the taxpayer did and how the taxpayer performed those activities, as submissions that merely repeat research credit legal definitions or statutory and regulatory language are deemed insufficient. Third, the taxpayer must provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year, which may be reported directly using Form 6765.

If the IRS determines that a refund claim filed during the administrative transition period (extended through January 10, 2027) is deficient, the agency issues Letter 6426C or Letter 6428, granting the taxpayer 45 days from the letter date to perfect the submission before formally rejecting the claim via Letter 6430 (No Consideration, Section 41 Claim)—a procedural determination that is not eligible for review by the IRS Independent Office of Appeals.
3. Revised Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) and Section G Business Component Reporting

Directly addressing the federal court's observation in Premier Tech that the IRS could revise its official tax forms to require project-level disclosures, the IRS overhauled Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, Rev. December 2025; Instructions posted February 6, 2026) to add Section E (Other Information), Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary), and Section G (Business Component Information).

While Section G is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless used to satisfy an amended return refund claim disclosure), it is mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 on original tax returns, unless the taxpayer meets one of two statutory/administrative exceptions: (a) the taxpayer is a Qualified Small Business (under IRC Section 41(h)(3)) electing the reduced payroll tax credit, or (b) the taxpayer has controlled-group QREs of $1.5 million or less on line 48, average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years of $50 million or less, and is reporting the credit on a timely filed original return. Filers required to complete Section G must report component-by-component QRE breakdowns—segregating direct research wages, direct supervision wages, direct support wages, supplies, computer rental/lease costs, and contract research—in descending order by total QREs for at least 80% of total QREs, reporting no more than 50 business components ("80% / Top 50"), with any remaining components reported in aggregate as "Aggregate Business Components". Consequently, granular project-level accounting and contemporaneous PoE documentation are now required for preparing standard original tax returns as well as amended refund claims.
C. Judicial Mandate for Contemporaneous Substantiation: Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner

The U.S. Tax Court's memorandum opinion in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, Docket No. 4759-22 (filed December 23, 2024, Judge Travis A. Greaves), illustrates the severe financial and legal consequences of claiming the R&D tax credit without contemporaneous PoE documentation.

Phoenix Design Group, Inc. (PDG) was a Tennessee consulting engineering firm taxed as a C corporation that designed mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) systems for commercial buildings, hospitals, and academic laboratories. In 2017, PDG engaged a third-party consulting firm (alliantgroup) to conduct a retrospective R&D study across 2012–2016 project documentation, claiming credits generated in 2013–2016 and utilized across tax years 2015–2019 attributable solely to employee wages. All of PDG's engineering projects followed a standard six-stage linear design workflow: (1) Basis of Design, (2) Schematic Design, (3) Design Development, (4) Construction Documents, (5) Bidding, and (6) Construction Administration. To streamline trial proceedings, PDG and the IRS agreed to try a non-binding three-project sample—the Gerald Champion Military Psychiatric Unit, Baptist Memorial Hospital–North Mississippi (Oxford), and the Vanderbilt University Engineering and Science Building—stipulating that if none of the three sampled projects involved qualified research, PDG would be liable for 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC Section 6662.

Although the IRS conceded the Technological Information Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)) and the Business Component Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)), the Tax Court ruled against PDG on every sampled project and upheld the 20% accuracy-related penalties based on three core evidentiary failures.

First, PDG failed to prove objective technical uncertainty at the project outset under the Section 174 Test. The court held that general building design complexity, tight client budgets, or evolving architectural floor plans before construction ends do not establish technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design if the information already available to the engineers—such as historical building load data, manufacturer equipment specifications, and standard engineering equations—is sufficient to determine the design. Nor did uncertainty regarding a single specialized room's equipment (such as a hospital's hybrid operating room) create technical uncertainty across an entire building's MEPF system.

Second, PDG failed to prove a systematic Process of Experimentation under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C). The court ruled that PDG's six-stage design workflow was linear rather than an iterative, hypothesis-driven evaluation of alternatives. Performing basic engineering calculations on available data—such as calculating approximate duct sizes from airflow requirements or referencing historical load data—is not an investigative activity or a process of experimentation reflecting the scientific method. Similarly, complying with building or energy codes or presenting utility options to a client without conducting an engineering evaluation of alternatives does not constitute experimentation.

Third, the absence of activity-level contemporaneous documentation precluded application of the shrinking-back rule. PDG's employee timesheets recorded generic phase labels such as "design" or "coordination" rather than linking hours to specific experimental tasks or subcomponents. When the overall MEPF system failed the 80% "substantially all" PoE test of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(6), the Tax Court examined whether it could apply the shrinking-back rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) to smaller subcomponents or specific disciplines such as mechanical, electrical, or plumbing. Because PDG lacked contemporaneous component-level and activity-level time and technical records—and because the shrinking-back rule can shrink back to a physical subcomponent or engineering discipline, but not to a linear design phase or to individual employees—the court was unable to salvage the claim even at a narrower subcomponent level.

body.text: III. Technical Scoping and Contemporaneous Documentation Mechanics
A. Formalizing Technical Uncertainty and Excluding Routine Engineering

Documenting the Process of Experimentation begins with scoping each project at inception to isolate genuine technical uncertainty from routine engineering, standard adaptation, or post-production maintenance. As the Tax Court's analysis in Phoenix Design Group and the IRS Audit Techniques Guides demonstrate, the presence of a demanding client specification, regulatory code, or complex system requirement does not automatically qualify or disqualify a project; rather, eligibility turns on whether the information available to the taxpayer at the outset failed to establish the capability, method, or appropriate design, and whether the taxpayer resolved that gap through a systematic evaluation of alternatives.

To formalize technical uncertainty in a manner that withstands IRS examination, project narratives must be drafted prospectively—before or during testing—around testable scientific or engineering hypotheses. Rather than stating vague commercial objectives such as making a software platform faster or improving a mechanical product, a compliant hypothesis defines the specific technical variable being manipulated and the measurable physical, chemical, engineering, or computational parameter being evaluated—for example, hypothesizing that a specific parallel-processing algorithm will reduce query latency by 15%, or testing whether a redesigned heat-sink fin geometry maintains thermal variance within 5% under peak load.

Equally important, scoping documentation must actively segregate and exclude activities that are statutorily barred under IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B), IRC Section 41(d)(4), and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c). Specifically, taxpayers must isolate and exclude research conducted after the beginning of commercial production under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(2), which encompasses any activities conducted after the business component meets basic functional and economic requirements, including preproduction planning, tooling up for production, trial production runs, routine troubleshooting of production equipment, and debugging post-release flaws. Similarly, project scoping must remove the adaptation of existing business components to a particular customer's requirement or need under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(B) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(3), as well as the duplication or reverse engineering of an existing business component in whole or in part from a physical examination, blueprints, specifications, or publicly available information under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(C) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(4). Furthermore, compliance controls must strip out efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, market research, routine data collection, and ordinary testing or inspection for quality control under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(5), alongside any work relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii).
B. Operationalizing Task-Level Contemporaneous Records

Capturing task-level evidence concurrently with R&D execution is particularly critical in modern software, high-technology, and manufacturing environments that utilize cross-functional teams and agile development workflows. Because agile sprints frequently interleave eligible experimentation (such as architectural modeling or algorithmic hypothesis testing) with non-qualifying tasks (such as routine bug fixes, user-interface styling, or customer configuration), the taxpayer's project-management and time-tracking systems must overlay granular activity codes tied directly to discrete business components and experimental phases.

Synthesizing specialized compliance documentation frameworks with Chapter 7 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities IRC § 41 (Substantiation and Recordkeeping) and revised Form 6765 Section G requirements yields four mandatory categories of contemporaneous records.

cells: 1. Project & Subcomponent Identification (Business Component)

Clear definition of each discrete business component (and its significant subcomponents to preserve the Shrinking-Back Rule under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)), including EIN, Principal Business Activity (PBA) code, and component type for Form 6765 Section G.

Project authorizations, Authorizations for Expenditure (AFEs), R&D budgets, work orders initiating research, statements of work (SOWs), formal third-party contracts (reviewed for funded-research risk under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H)), and memoranda of understanding.
2. Activity Description & Scientific Narrative (Process of Experimentation)

Detailed, non-boilerplate narrative of the systematic research activities performed per component: specific baseline uncertainty, hypotheses formulated, alternatives evaluated, experimental methodology, and test outcomes.

Technical scoping plans, progress reports, engineering/lab meeting minutes, CAD/CFD modeling and simulation files, field and laboratory verification data, prototype test logs, error/modification logs, and explicit records of failed trials and rejected alternatives.
3. Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) & Financial Ledger Tie-Out

Exact quantification and statutory segregation of in-house wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)), supplies (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)), off-premises computer rental/cloud dev leases (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)), and 65%/75%/100% contract research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3)).

Form W-2 Box 1 taxable wage registers (excluding pre-tax 401(k) and health benefits per IRC § 3401(a)), general ledger (GL) charts of accounts, supply purchase orders and invoices, cloud server invoices segregating dev vs. production hosting, and contractor agreements/Form 1099s.
4. Contemporaneous Time & Nexus Evidence

Concurrent, time-stamped records establishing the quantitative nexus between employee labor/costs and specific experimental steps, proving both the ≥ 80% component PoE test (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)) and employee wage allocations (26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)).

Time-stamped task logs (e.g., Jira tickets, Git version-control commits, ERP/PeopleSoft project-activity timesheets) linking employee hours to specific experimental tests (e.g., "Activity 1.2: Thermal Testing") rather than broad project names.

Records generic timesheet buckets such as "Project A – 8 hours" or linear phases like "Design / Coordination".
Links employee timesheets directly to discrete experimental tasks and subcomponents (e.g., "Activity 1.2: Thermal Testing").

body.text: C. Overcoming the Expense Segregation Trap: IRC Section 3401(a) Wages and Foreign Research

Even when a taxpayer's technical narrative satisfies the Four-Part Test, R&D credit claims frequently suffer substantial audit adjustments due to improper financial allocation and the inclusion of statutorily ineligible expenses in the QRE pool. Two statutory exclusions require strict accounting segregation prior to filing.

First, under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(D)(i), the term "wages" for R&D credit purposes has the exact meaning given by IRC Section 3401(a)—namely, taxable remuneration subject to federal income tax withholding, as reported in Box 1 of Form W-2. As explicitly confirmed in Chapter 4a of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities IRC § 41 – Qualified Research Expenses, qualified wages include taxable base wages, taxable bonuses, and taxable stock option spread in the year exercised (provided the underlying grant-year services were qualified services), but exclude all amounts not subject to income tax withholding under IRC Section 3401(a). Consequently, pre-tax employee 401(k) elective deferrals, employer 401(k) matching contributions, employer-paid health insurance premiums, pre-tax cafeteria or medical plan deductions, and other non-taxable fringe benefits do not qualify as QREs, even when paid to an engineer or scientist who spent 100% of their time conducting qualified experimentation. Because corporate general ledger payroll accounts typically bundle gross salaries, employer 401(k) matches, and health insurance costs together, claiming unadjusted general ledger labor totals without reconciling to Form W-2 Box 1 wages triggers an immediate audit adjustment.

Second, under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F), "qualified research" excludes any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States. As clarified in Chapter 5c of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide, the IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F) foreign-research exclusion applies to both in-house employee research and third-party contract research, and bars the credit even if the offshore research is performed by American citizens or paid for by an American corporate taxpayer. Moreover, under current IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) and the December 2025 Form 6765 Instructions, expenditures must qualify as domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A.
D. Hypothetical Worked Example: Component-Level PoE and Wage QRE Substantiation

To illustrate how contemporaneous task logs and payroll cleansing interact under the statutory and regulatory rules, consider the following worked example for a United States manufacturing corporation developing a new business component (Component ID: TCM-01, Thermal Control Module) during the taxable year.
Step 1: Testing the Business Component Under the 80% PoE Rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6))

Suppose the taxpayer's contemporaneous project-tracking system logs a total of 900 hours of research activities for TCM-01 that satisfy the Section 174/174A uncertainty test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)) and are not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4). Those 900 hours consist of 320 hours in Activity 1.1 (formulating hypotheses and conducting computational fluid dynamics thermal modeling of four alternative heat-sink fin geometries), 440 hours in Activity 1.2 (iterative environmental chamber testing of Prototype Alternatives 1 through 4, logging three failed runs with thermal variance exceeding 5% and one final passing run), and 140 hours in Activity 1.3 (initial baseline literature review and post-experiment technical summary compilation that satisfies IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) and is not excluded under Section 41(d)(4), but is not itself an evaluative trial).

Applying the activity-level "substantially all" fraction under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(6), the numerator (elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose) equals 320 hours + 440 hours = 760 hours, and the denominator (all research activities for the component satisfying Section 174(a)/174A and not excluded under Section 41(d)(4)) equals 320 hours + 440 hours + 140 hours = 900 hours:
TCM-01 PoE Activity Fraction = (320 hours + 440 hours) ÷ (320 hours + 440 hours + 140 hours) = 760 hours ÷ 900 hours = 84.44%

Because 84.44% is ≥ 80.0%, Component TCM-01 satisfies the "substantially all" Process of Experimentation requirement of IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(6), meaning all 900 hours of research activity on TCM-01 qualify at the business-component level.
Step 2: Cleansing Payroll Costs and Allocating Employee Wage QREs (IRC § 3401(a) & 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d))

Suppose three personnel performed work connected to TCM-01 and other company operations during the taxable year. IV. Case Study in Audit-Resilient Substantiation
A. Prospective On-Site Scoping and Jurisdictional Terminology Alignment

Deploying domain engineers and scientists at project inception ensures that technical narratives isolate specific baseline uncertainties and log experimental iterations using scientific terminology aligned with the evaluation standards of IRS Engineering Specialists.

In Australia's R&D Tax Incentive (administered by AusIndustry and reviewed by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal), the governing statute divides eligible work into "core R&D activities" and "supporting R&D activities". In the United States under IRC Section 41(d)(2) and Form 6765 Section G, however, the mandatory statutory unit of analysis is the "business component," with employee labor categorized into direct conduct, direct supervision, and direct support of qualified research under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B). Second, international compliance materials occasionally refer to cost reviews by "Chartered Accountants (CA)/CPAs" and sign-offs by a "Registered R&D Tax Agent/Specialist". In United States federal practice before the IRS, the corresponding recognized professional tax credentials are Certified Public Accountants (CPAs) and Enrolled Agents (EAs).
B. Automated Contemporaneous Compliance via TaxTrex

According to the platform's technical specifications, TaxTrex employs a real-time "prospective documentation" architecture in which autonomous AI agents and automated survey systems prompt technical personnel throughout the tax year to record baseline uncertainties, hypotheses tested, and experimental outcomes concurrently with project execution, rather than relying on retroactive reconstruction at tax filing time.

In addition to narrative capture, the platform ingests task-level project data and synchronizes with corporate accounting software to link qualified expenses directly to R&D activities and substantiate IRS Form 6765. The software also incorporates an "Intelligent Risk Assessment" feature and Four-Part Test compliance heuristics to evaluate claim risk early in the documentation lifecycle.
C. The Mandatory Six-Eye Review and ISO 31000 Risk Management Framework

cells: 1. Technical Engineering & Scientific Review (Technical Gate)

Qualified Engineer & Scientist (in U.S. materials, structured as First Set of Eyes: Qualified Engineer, and Second Set of Eyes: Scientist; in Australian materials, Qualified Engineer who is a Registered R&D Tax Agent).

Validates that each business component faces genuine technical uncertainty (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)), relies on hard science (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)), and documents a systematic hypothesis-test-analysis cycle (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)), rejecting claims that show only final commercial results without iterative trial/failure records.

Disallowance under the Section 174 Uncertainty Test or Process of Experimentation Test (as occurred in Phoenix Design Group, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, and Little Sandy Coal, 62 F.4th 287), and misclassification of routine engineering or quality control as R&D.
2. Financial & Cost Accounting Review (Costing Gate)
Certified Public Accountant (CPA), Enrolled Agent (EA), or Chartered Accountant (CA).

Audits the general ledger tie-out, reconciles employee wages strictly to taxable Form W-2 Box 1 compensation under IRC § 3401(a), removes non-taxable benefits (401(k), health insurance) and foreign research costs (IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)), verifies the 80% wage threshold (26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)), and checks prototype depreciation vs. supply expensing.
Financial overstatements, inclusion of excluded fringe benefits or foreign labor, loss of the "nexus" link between QREs and QRAs (RCCATG), and 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662.
3. Regulatory & Quality Control Sign-Off (Compliance Gate)
Registered Tax Specialist / CPA / Enrolled Agent / Senior Quality Control Principal (augmented by creditARMOR compliance heuristics).

Confirms adherence to current tax legislation, verifies third-party contracts against the funded-research exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H)), and checks compliance with IRS upfront refund disclosure rules (IR-2021-203 / June 2024 update) and Form 6765 Section E/F/G reporting prerequisites.

Upfront procedural rejection (Letter 6428 / Letter 6430), disqualification of funded contract research, and conflicts of interest (mitigated via structural reviewer independence and avoidance of contingent fees).

body.text: Two technical clarifications govern the institutional application of ISO 31000:2009 in U.S. tax compliance. First, regarding standard currency, according to the International Organization for Standardization Technical Committee ISO/TC 262 (Risk Management), ISO 31000:2009 (Risk management – Principles and guidelines) was formally revised and superseded by ISO 31000:2018 in mid-February 2018. Second, while advisory literature occasionally suggests that an internationally certified risk management system signals to IRS auditors to classify a claim as low-risk, as a matter of official IRS examination procedure under Internal Revenue Manual IRM 4.46.3.7.3, IRM 4.46.3.7.6, and the IRS Audit Techniques Guides, the IRS does not classify a return or refund claim as low-risk based on a tax preparer's ISO certification. Instead, IRS classifiers and examiners risk-assess research credit claims based on the taxpayer's Form 6765 disclosures, industry and financial risk indicators, and the objective adequacy of the taxpayer's underlying contemporaneous books and records under IRC Section 6001.
V. Strategic Synthesis and Actionable Compliance Recommendations
A. Core Pillars of Defensible Process of Experimentation Documentation

Synthesizing the statutory mandates of IRC Section 41(d), the U.S. Tax Court's evidentiary holdings in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2024-113), the Seventh Circuit's quantitative standard in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287), and the IRS's upfront disclosure rules (IR-2021-203, the June 18, 2024 refund claim update, and Form 6765 Section G) establishes three foundational pillars for documenting the Process of Experimentation.

First, taxpayers must execute prospective technical scoping at the business-component and subcomponent level, defining each discrete business component under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B)—and its most significant subsets of elements under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2)—at project inception, and documenting why the information available to the taxpayer failed to establish capability, method, or appropriate design under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(3)(i). Second, organizations must enforce contemporaneous capture of the hypothesis-trial-evaluation cycle and dual 80% thresholds under IRC Section 6001 and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(d), recording testable hypotheses, modeling or simulation parameters, systematic trial-and-error iterations, and failed tests or rejected alternatives under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) while tracking task-level hours to prove both that ≥ 80% of each business component's research activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(6) and how each employee's qualified service hours compare against the 80% employee wage threshold under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(2). Third, claims must undergo interdisciplinary quality assurance and strict expense segregation prior to filing, combining engineering and scientific review of the PoE narrative with CPA or Enrolled Agent verification that non-taxable benefits (such as 401(k) contributions and health insurance premiums) under IRC Section 3401(a), foreign research costs under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F), and non-qualifying post-production or routine tasks under IRC Section 41(d)(4) have been excluded from the QRE calculation.
B. Actionable Implementation Checklist for Tax and Engineering Leadership

To operationalize these statutory and judicial standards and prepare for mandatory Form 6765 Section G reporting (effective for tax years beginning after 2025) and potential IRS examinations, corporate tax and engineering leadership should execute the five-step compliance protocol detailed below.

cells: 1. Restructure Time-Tracking and ERP/Project Codes

Eliminate single-bucket "R&D" or generic linear phase-based ("Schematic Design," "Coordination") timesheet codes. Configure Jira, Git, or ERP time-tracking systems so engineers log hours against specific business components, significant subcomponents, and discrete experimental activities (distinguishing direct experimentation, direct supervision, and direct support from routine code compliance or quality control).
Form 6765 Section G Column 49(c) alphanumeric component IDs; 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) Shrinking-Back Rule; 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) ≥ 80% Component PoE Test.
2. Mandate Pre-Test Hypothesis Scoping & Failure Logs

Train R&D managers, software architects, and lead engineers that successful commercial outcomes do not prove qualified research. Require a brief, time-stamped technical scoping entry at project kickoff stating the specific design uncertainty and testable hypothesis, and preserve all simulation runs, prototype test failures, and rejected design alternatives in a centralized repository.
IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) & (C); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)–(ii) & (a)(5)(i); Phoenix Design Group, T.C. Memo. 2024-113.
3. Automate Contemporaneous Evidence Collection

Deploy structured compliance software (such as TaxTrex or integrated project-management capture tools) to extract contemporaneous technical artifacts and conduct periodic automated surveys during the tax year, eliminating retrospective year-end estimation.
IRC § 6001; 26 CFR § 1.6001-1(a); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d); IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG).
4. Enforce Payroll & General Ledger Cleansing

Establish an accounting reconciliation worksheet operated by a CPA or Enrolled Agent that maps claimed wage QREs directly to Form W-2 Box 1 taxable wages, stripping out all pre-tax 401(k) deferrals, employer retirement matches, employer-paid health insurance, non-taxable fringe benefits, and offshore labor or contractor expenses.
5. Institute a Pre-Filing Interdisciplinary ("Six-Eye") Gate

Require formal pre-submission sign-off from (a) a qualified domain engineer/scientist validating technical uncertainty and PoE trial records, (b) a CPA or Enrolled Agent verifying QRE calculations and cost nexus, and (c) a tax compliance specialist confirming adherence to Form 6765 Section G ("80% / Top 50" component reporting) and the three mandatory upfront refund-claim disclosures.
